question: Which statement best describes Suspense boundaries?
options: These two are complementary, not interchangeable. Suspense handles the pending state (a thrown promise); failures — a rejected promise or a chunk that fails to load — surface as thrown errors that only an Error Boundary can catch. A production region typically pairs a Suspense boundary for loading with an Error Boundary for failure so each is handled by the right mechanism.

A <Suspense> component defines a boundary: a unit of UI that 'loads together'. When any descendant suspends, React walks up to the nearest boundary above it and renders that boundary's fallback instead of the unfinished subtree. The boundary must be an ancestor of the suspending component — placing it below has no effect, and having none at all causes React to throw.

The JSX passed to the fallback prop is shown while children are suspended. A good fallback is a skeleton that reserves the same layout space as the real content, which prevents cumulative layout shift (CLS) when the content swaps in. Avoid bare spinners for content-heavy regions — skeletons communicate structure and feel faster.

Under the hood, a component suspends by throwing a promise-like value to signal 'not ready yet'; React catches it at the nearest boundary and retries rendering once it resolves. React.lazy components always support this. Plain React does NOT let arbitrary fetches suspend — data Suspense requires a framework or library integration (Next.js, Relay) or the use() hook fed a framework-provided resource.

With renderToPipeableStream (Node) or renderToReadableStream (edge), the server sends the HTML shell immediately and emits the fallback HTML for any not-yet-ready Suspense boundary. As suspended content resolves on the server, React streams additional HTML chunks plus tiny inline scripts that swap each fallback for the real content — no client round-trip. This means one slow data dependency no longer blocks the entire page from reaching the user.

By default, an update that causes a component to suspend immediately shows the boundary's fallback — which produces jarring spinner flashes during navigation even when content resolves almost instantly. Wrapping the update in startTransition (or useTransition) marks it non-urgent, so React keeps the existing content visible and interactive while the new content loads in the background, only falling back if there is nothing to keep showing.

Choosing where and how many boundaries to place is a real design decision. Too few means coarse loading and a shared failure blast radius; too many causes skeleton churn and layout thrash. Render the instant shell outside any boundary, then group related content per boundary so each independently-loading region — a metrics panel, an activity feed — reveals on its own timeline.
